name: trigno_simd_cpp (SIMD trigonometric approximations, Goyal & Arora)
workload: 1000 random double-precision angles in [-1e6, 1e6] (fixed seed 2024873), each evaluated 1e5 times; wall-clock execution time of proposed piecewise SIMD sin/cos/tan vs inbuilt C++ std::sin/cos/tan
claimed_speedup: Mean speed-up ratio (std_time/observed_time) vs inbuilt: sin 5.49x, cos 5.52x, tan 4.44x
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900HX (8 cores/16 threads, 3301 MHz max), 16GB RAM, Windows 10 Home Single Language, 64-bit
tradeoffs: Approximate (piecewise rational sin/cos with max relative error ~0.004; tan max absolute error ~0.27 near asymptotes vs 148+ for a degree-9 Taylor baseline); not IEEE correctly-rounded; internally uses a fast inverse-square-root (FISR) hack in place of sqrt/division; the published API is scalar (one angle in, one double out) even though the implementation uses AVX2/FMA internally, so real batched throughput may differ from the reported per-call microbenchmark
caveats: arXiv preprint (cs.MS, Feb 2025), not confirmed peer-reviewed or published elsewhere; the benchmark and the paper are by the same two authors (first-party), though the code and full methodology (compiler flags, CPU, seed) are public and reproducible, which is why it is scored tier A rather than C per the rubric; the code repo itself has only 7 GitHub stars; the paper calls the baseline 'inbuilt C++ functions' without naming libstdc++ explicitly, inferred from the stated g++ toolchain
found_via: WebSearch: 'SIMD math library faster than libm exp log sin cos paper' -> arXiv:2502.10831 'A Novel SIMD-Optimized Implementation for Fast and Memory-Efficient Trigonometric Computation'; code repo URL resolved from the paper's reference [11]

name: FABE13-HX
baseline: libm sin/cos/sincos (the implementation <cmath>'s std::sin/std::cos ultimately call into)
workload: sin/cos/sincos evaluated over arrays ranging from 10 to 1e9 doubles, compared against system libm (GNU math.h on Linux, macOS system math.h)
claimed_speedup: Up to 8.4x faster than libm on x86 (AVX2+FMA, Clang/AppleClang); 4.36-5.82x on ARM64/NEON depending on array size, max relative error <= 2e-11
hardware: No specific CPU model/SKU given; platforms described only as 'Replit cloud Linux (AVX2+FMA)', 'MacBook Pro 16-inch (AVX2+FMA)', and generic 'ARM64/NEON'
tradeoffs: Approximate, not correctly rounded; built with -Ofast -ffast-math, which relaxes IEEE-754 semantics and can itself inflate speed deltas versus a strict-mode libm build; exposes a scalar API (fabe13_sin(double) etc.) despite internally using SIMD
caveats: First-party README benchmark only; no independent reproduction found; no specific CPU model stated for any platform, only generic descriptions, so tier is capped below A; the MIT LICENSE file actually lives at fabe13-old/LICENSE (a subdirectory) rather than the repo root, which is why GitHub's repo metadata API reports no detected license even though MIT license text exists in the repo; author's own branding ('Ψ-Hyperbasis algorithm', 'Lightcap Initiative') and lack of any third-party citation or discussion found make this an unverified, low-notability first-party source
found_via: WebSearch: 'SIMD math library faster than libm exp log sin cos paper'

name: NumKong (formerly SimSIMD)
baseline: hand-written C++ dot-product/reduction loop, semantically equivalent to std::inner_product / std::transform_reduce, auto-vectorized by GCC 12 -O3
workload: Half-precision (f16) inner product, cosine distance, squared Euclidean distance, and Jensen-Shannon divergence over vectors, single-threaded, on Intel Sapphire Rapids
claimed_speedup: f16 kernels vs GCC-12-compiled auto-vectorized f16 loop: Inner Product 31x, Cosine Distance 20x, Euclidean Distance^2 36x, Jensen-Shannon Divergence 118x
compiler_and_flags: GCC 12 (exact optimization flags beyond auto-vectorization not stated in README)
hardware: Intel Sapphire Rapids (Xeon generation family; exact SKU not stated), single-threaded
tradeoffs: The comparison baseline is GCC's auto-vectorization of a plain scalar loop written in the project's own bench harness, not literally a call through <numeric>'s std::transform_reduce/std::inner_product, so the baseline match is inferred rather than exact; library trades a very large API surface (2000+ kernels across 15+ numeric types) and wider mixed-precision accumulators for speed; repo also publishes a much larger benchmark table for its element-wise trigonometric kernels (sin/cos/atan), but those are only benchmarked against the project's own non-SIMD 'serial' reimplementation of the same SLEEF-derived algorithm rather than against std::sin/cos/<cmath>, so that portion was deliberately excluded from this entry
caveats: Baseline is inferred (GCC-compiled raw loop, confirmed by reading bench/bench_cross_serial.cpp which contains no literal std:: calls), not a literal std:: facility call in the benchmark source; exact GCC flags and CPU SKU are not given, so tier is capped at C rather than A/B; project was recently renamed from 'SimSIMD' to 'NumKong' within the same GitHub repository
found_via: WebSearch: 'SIMD linear algebra library benchmark faster than valarray' -> blog.lancedb.com 'My SIMD Is Faster than Yours' referenced the SimSIMD/NumKong family; verified directly on github.com/ashvardanian/SimSIMD README and bench/ sources

name: Axiom (C++ tensor library)
baseline: Eigen3 element-wise unary math ops (sin/cos/exp/log/etc.), the de facto standard replacement for hand-rolled std::transform+<cmath> loops in C++ numeric code
workload: Element-wise unary math ops (exp, log, sqrt, sin, cos, tanh, abs, neg, relu, sigmoid) over a 4096x4096 tensor, GB/s throughput, vs Eigen3, PyTorch, NumPy
claimed_speedup: sin: 26.0 GB/s (Axiom) vs 11.0 GB/s (Eigen3), ~2.4x (derived from page data); cos: 25.2 vs 11.0, ~2.3x (derived); exp: 23.0 vs 16.4, ~1.4x (derived); log: 17.0 vs 13.1, ~1.3x (derived). Same table shows sqrt and tanh as SLOWER than Eigen3, so the win is op-specific, not universal
hardware: Apple M4 Pro (per README headline); the benchmark doc's own 'Test Environment' section only states 'Darwin 25.3.0, arm64'
tradeoffs: Not a std::-drop-in: NumPy/PyTorch-like whole-tensor API, no scalar single-value entry point; on macOS Axiom itself delegates BLAS-level and possibly vectorized-math work to Apple's Accelerate framework, so part of the win may reflect Accelerate/vForce vs Eigen's own vectorization rather than a novel Axiom algorithm; several unary ops (sqrt, tanh) are slower than Eigen3 in the same table
caveats: Benchmark is entirely first-party (project's own docs/BENCHMARKS.md, auto-generated by its own `make benchmark`), not independently reproduced; compiler and optimization flags are not stated anywhere in the repo's benchmark docs, so tier is capped at C; the 'M4 Pro' CPU claim appears only in the README headline while the benchmark doc's own 'Test Environment' section is vague ('Darwin 25.3.0 arm64'); comparison baseline (Eigen3) is a library, not literally std::transform/<cmath>, so this is an inferred rather than exact baseline match, confidence lowered accordingly
found_via: HN Algolia (hn.algolia.com/api/v1/search?query=SIMD%20linear%20algebra%20library): 'Show HN: Axiom – C++ tensor library with NumPy's API, optimized for Apple Silicon'
